messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: Solving two regressions simultaneously
parts:
Is it possible to solve two linear regressions simultaneously using STAN, for example, I have:

(1) r = Xf + e

and 

(2) h = Hg + u

where f = H^Tr

I can solve (1) to estimate f = H^Tr where H = X(X^TX)^-1 and using H, I can solve for g but I would like to solve them simultaneously. Perhaps STAN is a way to go. I have attempted writing a STAN model as follows:

data{
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] X;
  vector[N] r;
  vector[N] h;
}
parameters{
  matrix[N, K] H;
  vector[K] g;
  real<lower=0> sigma_e; // no prior available
  real<lower=0> sigma_u; // no prior available
}
transformed parameters{
  vector[K] f;
  f = H' * r
  // ideally a good constraint X'H = I
  //X' * H = diag_matrix(rep_vector(1, N));
}
model{
  r - X * f ~ normal(0, sigma_e);
  h - H * g ~ normal(0, sigma_u);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving two regressions simultaneously
parts:
You can get maximum likelihood estimates out of our
optimizer if that's what you meant. Or you can get
a Bayesian posterior estimate.

And yes, what you have will work, but we'd write

> model{
> r - X * f ~ normal(0, sigma_e);
> h - H * g ~ normal(0, sigma_u);
> }

more generatively as the equivalent (in terms of log density):

r ~ normal(X * H' * r, sigma_e);

h ~ normal(H * g, sigma_u);

And we'd call those sigmas sigma_r and sigma_h.

You don't have to define f = H' * r, but you can if you want
to save the values for posterior analysis.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving two regressions simultaneously
parts:
Out of curiosity, what is the model being used for? Typically, even if you don't have an informative prior for either of the sigmas you will have at least some minimal prior information, which can be helpful for stabilizing computations (and avoiding overfitting).

Jonah

messages.author: fbff4100433066b4
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving two regressions simultaneously
parts:
This is related to listed equity portfolio attribution. I am trying to attribute portfolio returns (h^Tr) to factors in exposure matrix X, in this process H is a matrix whose columns are factor portfolios to compute factor returns f. Using H,  I can also compute how my portfolio h is spanned by factor portfolios in H, So g is my exposure to various factors, I can get k factor's contribution to portfolio return as g_k times f_k. u is the residual portfolio and u^Tr is the residual return that factors cannot explain.

In a two step process H is tailored to factors and is 'unaware' of h, and this results in large u. In a joint regression I was hoping to 'somewhat' tailor H also to h. 

I still need more ideas to reduce the variance of H estimated in the joint regression.
